latin: Qui intellexerit cur sit dictum quod Moyses abscondit faciem suam, et quod Ezechias uertit facies suas ad parietem, sciet quae esse debeat orantis habitudo et dispositio.
translation: Whoever understands why it is said that Moses hid his face, and that Hezekiah turned his face to the wall, will know what the bearing and disposition of one who prays ought to be.
translation_note: The two scriptural allusions are Exod. 3:6 (Moses hiding his face) and 2 Kings 20:2-3 (Vulgate 4 Kings/Malachim 20:2-3, Hezekiah turning to the wall) (farmer1998:18220).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch11, from Latin at farmer1998:18190
doctrine: Farmer glosses the thesis by its two scriptural allusions, Exod. 3:6 and 2 Kings 20:2-3, and reads it as one of several theses suggesting that God at his highest lies beyond human understanding, implying the need, at the highest stages of the mystical ascent, to set aside ordinary forms of knowledge; he cross-references 26.5 and 11>35 among others (farmer1998:18220).
context: Farmer cross-references 11>35, on nothing being understood to proceed from God considered in himself as infinite and one (farmer1998:27129), and 26.5, on the intelligible order lying above every intellectual hierarchy (farmer1998:17143) (farmer1998:18220).
historiography: Wirszubski transcribes the thesis in full as his 'Conclusio XXXIV' (wirszubski1989:2636, 2639) and elsewhere states that it was in Recanati, and not by his own wits, that Pico found the combination of texts that brought out the proper attitude at prayer, adding that it was because he read the Zohar through Recanati's eyes that Pico understood it so well (wirszubski1989:3140).

quotations.text: It was likewise in Recanati, and not by his own wits, that Pico found the shrewd combination of texts that brought out some particular points, such as the proper attitude at prayer (Conclusio xxxiv).
